remote-state.name: Terraform state is kept in a remote backend
remote-state.description: Every live Terraform root stores its state in a remote backend, and no state file is left in the checkout.
remote-state.remediation:
Store state in a shared backend with locking and encryption:

```hcl
terraform {
  backend "s3" {
    bucket       = "company-terraform-state"
    key          = "live/network.tfstate"
    region       = "eu-west-1"
    encrypt      = true
    use_lockfile = true
  }
}
```

Then keep state files out of the repository:

```bash
printf '*.tfstate\n*.tfstate.backup\n' >> .gitignore
git rm --cached terraform.tfstate
```

Local state is one lost laptop away from being gone, and two concurrent applies overwrite each other with nothing to stop them. A state file in the repository is worse than lost state: it contains every attribute of every resource, including the ones marked `sensitive`, and anyone who can read the repository can read it.

checkStateFiles.description: Whether a `.tfstate` or `.tfstate.backup` file in the working tree is a violation. The collector reads the working tree, not the git index, so a developer who has run `terraform apply` locally has one even though nobody committed it. In CI the checkout matches the repository, so the two are the same.

modulePaths.description: Comma separated globs naming directories that hold reusable modules rather than live roots. A module declares no backend and pins nothing, so it is not judged here. A directory another root takes on with a local `source` is recognised as a module whether or not it matches.

providers-pinned.name: Terraform providers are pinned
providers-pinned.description: Every provider a live Terraform root requires is pinned to one exact version, and the lock file that resolves them is committed.

requireLockfile.description: Whether a root that requires providers must commit a `.terraform.lock.hcl`. A root that requires no providers is never asked for one.

no-plaintext-secrets.name: Terraform variables holding secrets are marked sensitive
no-plaintext-secrets.description: Every Terraform variable named like a credential declares `sensitive = true`.
no-plaintext-secrets.remediation:
Mark the variable as sensitive, and don't give it a default:

```hcl
variable "db_password" {
  type      = string
  sensitive = true
}
```

Pass the value in from the secret store your pipeline already uses, as an environment variable, instead of from a `.tfvars` file anyone can commit:

```bash
TF_VAR_db_password="$(aws ssm get-parameter --name /company/db/password --with-decryption --query Parameter.Value --output text)" terraform apply
```

`sensitive = true` redacts the value in plans and CLI output. It doesn't encrypt it in state, so the backend still needs to encrypt. Plans are the exposure people miss: a pull request comment that quotes a plan publishes whatever the plan printed.

patterns.description: Comma separated glob patterns, matched case-insensitively against the name of every `variable` block. Only names are checked: the collector never collects defaults, because a default can be the credential itself.

state-locking.name: Terraform state is locked
state-locking.description: Every live Terraform root declares state locking, so two applies cannot write the same state at once.

state-encrypted.description: Every live Terraform root declares an encrypted backend, so its state isn't stored in the clear in its bucket.

modules-pinned.name: Terraform modules are pinned
modules-pinned.description: Every module a Terraform root pulls from a registry or a git URL names a version, so the same commit always resolves to the same module code.
modules-pinned.remediation:
Pin the modules named in the violations. For a registry source, pin with `version`:

```hcl
module "vpc" {
  source  = "terraform-aws-modules/vpc/aws"
  version = "5.8.1"
}
```

For a git source, pin with a ref in the URL. A tag isn't enough, because a tag can move:

```hcl
module "vpc" {
  source = "git::https://github.com/company/terraform-vpc.git?ref=6f3a1c2d9b8e4f7a0c5d2e1b3a4f5c6d7e8f9a0b"
}
```

With an unpinned module, the plan you reviewed and the plan that was applied can come from different code. A module in this repository, referenced with a relative `source`, is already pinned by the commit and isn't checked.

allowMovableRefs.description: Whether a git source pinned to a tag or branch instead of a commit SHA counts as pinned. `false` requires a 40 character SHA, the only ref nobody can move.
